← Holiday light bid calculator

How much to charge to hang Christmas lights

Holiday lighting contractors get shopped on a published $3 / lineal foot Christmas light hang Facebook special. Those numbers cannot see the take-down or the stories. A 1-story ranch C9 hang-only is a different job from a two-story Victorian with icicles, tree wraps, January take-down, and off-season storage.

Open the free holiday light bid calculator

Price the hang and the take-down, not the $3 dump

Holiday lights are an eave, then a scope, then how you reach it. Lineal feet is the run. Hang-only is clips on customer-owned C9. Hang-and-takedown is a second trip in January. Full service — contractor lights plus storage until next year — is another crew package. One-story is a ladder. Two-story needs a taller ladder or a small lift. Three-story is a lift.

Hang-only is not full service

The cheap special is almost always C9 on a 1-story ranch, no take-down, no trees, no lift. A two-story hang-and-takedown is a different crew day. Matching a hang per-foot number on a full-service Victorian is how a sold light job becomes a January loss when take-down eats the margin.

This is not landscape lighting or soffit wrap

Landscape lighting is low-voltage path and uplights. Soffit and fascia is wrap or replace of the eave board. Gutter install is a K-style trough. Exterior painting is a coat on elevations. This prices holiday lights: hang, take-down, and extras. The eave here is the roofline you clip lights to, not those other jobs.

Walk-away price

Load the wage with payroll burden. Add overhead as a share of direct cost. Then take margin as a share of the customer’s price, not a markup on cost. The walk-away number is total cost. A proposed price under that number loses money before you take anything out of it.

This page is a walkthrough of the arithmetic in the holiday light bid calculator. It is not an electrical design, a load calculation, a permit determination, or a price you should copy onto a contract.

Common questions

How much should I charge to hang Christmas lights?

Charge from eave lineal feet, scope, stories, and extras — not a published $3 / LF hang special. A 1-story ranch C9 hang-only is a different job from a two-story Victorian with icicles, tree wraps, January take-down, and off-season storage.

Is hang-only the same bid as full-service holiday lights?

No. Hang-only is clips on customer-owned lights. Hang-and-takedown is a second crew day in January. Full service — contractor lights plus storage until next year — is another one still. Matching a hang special on a full-service job is how a sold light job becomes a January loss when take-down eats the margin.

How do stories change a holiday-light price?

A 1-story ranch is an extension ladder. A 2-story house needs a taller ladder or a small lift. A 3-story or steep eave needs a lift. Height does not live in a published per-foot dump.

Is this the same as landscape lighting or soffit wrap?

No. Landscape lighting is low-voltage path and uplights. Soffit and fascia is wrap or replace of the eave board. Gutter install is a K-style trough. This prices holiday lights: hang, take-down, and extras.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is. It is not electrical, lighting-design, building-code, legal, tax, or financial advice. Verify every figure against your own light invoices and crew times before relying on it.

    Common questions

    Why can a flyer advertise “$3 a foot, hang-only”?

    Because that is a real number for a real, narrow job: the first preset here, a one-story ranch, 140 feet of C9 on clips, customer-owned lights, no take-down. Hang-only skips the 45% take-down ratio and the full-service 50% ratio entirely — there is simply no second trip to price. Add a January take-down, a second story, or icicle lights and the flyer’s number stops describing your job; the gap is not padding, it is the trip the flyer left out.

    Why does hang-and-takedown cost more than twice a hang-only special?

    Because take-down is not half the hang labor, it is 45–50% of the hang-and-access hours billed as a second visit — a separate trip, separate travel, separate ladder-setting — on top of the original hang. Full service adds a third cost on top of that: contractor-owned lights at $2.60 a foot and a flat $95 off-season storage invoice, since nothing goes back to the customer’s garage.

    What does a second story actually add?

    1.6 access hours and $0.014 per foot before a single extra light is hung, plus a $165 lift invoice the calculator bills as a flat material cost. Three-story or a lift-required roofline doubles the access hours to 3.2, the per-foot premium to $0.028, and the lift invoice to $390. That is ladder-setting and working off height, not lineal footage — which is why the same 180 feet costs more on a colonial than a ranch.

    What changes between C9, icicle, and commercial-grade lights?

    C9 on clips is the base case: zero extra hours, zero extra material, because it is what the hang-hours-per-foot rate already assumes. Icicle adds 0.02 hours and $1.40 of material per foot for the denser clip-and-hook run. Commercial-grade LED C9 adds less labor — 0.008 hours per foot — but more material, $3.20 a foot, because the fixture itself costs more than the extra clipping time.

    How are peaks, trees, bushes, and columns priced?

    Each is its own line, not folded into the per-foot rate: a peak or gable adds 0.35 hours and $18 of material, a tree wrap adds 0.9 hours and $42, a bush or shrub net adds 0.25 hours and $14, and a column wrap adds 0.2 hours and $12. A timer or photocell adds 0.35 hours and a $28 invoice, and a steep-pitch roof adds a flat 0.8 access hours on top of the story premium. None of these move with eave footage, so a small house with six trees can cost more than a long, plain roofline.

    Is my data uploaded anywhere?

    No account and no network requests — the calculator runs entirely in your browser. Your bid is saved in this browser’s local storage so it is still here next visit. The optional usage counter records only which features were used and the day, never your footage, wages, or prices, and you can turn it off from the checkbox in the footer.

vs-a-flat-3-per-lf-special.html.text:
← Holiday Light Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat $3/LF Christmas light special

“$3 a lineal foot to hang Christmas lights” is not a price for a holiday lighting install — it is a price for one specific run, quietly applied to every eave the truck pulls up to.

What a flat $3/LF special is

A flat per-foot special is the fastest way to quote: one headline number on a postcard, a Facebook ad, or a yard sign, read off and repeated. Owners shop it because it is easy to compare between bids, and it is the number a homeowner holding a competitor's flyer will ask you to match on their own house.

The number behind it was set for one job — usually a ground-reachable 1-story ranch, hang-only on customer-owned C9, no January take-down trip, no storage — and then reused for every roofline afterward, whether or not the next house looks anything like a hang-only ranch.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the eave lineal feet, the scope — hang-only, hang-and-takedown, or full-service storage — stories, light type, peaks, tree wraps, bush nets, column wraps, a timer, a steep pitch, and travel miles, plus your loaded labor and overhead. It prices the scope, the story access, and every extra separately, and returns a walk-away price and an extra-work share below which the job loses money — for this house, not a generic one.

What a flat $3/LF special doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same per-foot number whether the job is hang-only on a 1-story ranch or full-service on a 2-story Victorian with icicle lights, take-down, and storage. Prices the scope from the entered hang, take-down, and storage selection, so the two jobs above come out at different numbers instead of one.
Has no line for a second visit, so a January take-down trip — a second crew day and a second round of travel — is quoted the same as a job that only ever gets hung once. Prices take-down hours as a ratio of the hang labor and adds a second travel trip whenever take-down is selected, so the second visit shows up instead of being absorbed.
Assumes a 1-story extension ladder, so a 2-story taller ladder or a 3-story lift gets quoted the same as a job that needs neither. Adds access hours and a lift invoice only for the stories entered, so a taller reach costs more than a ranch.
Prices "Christmas lights" as one flat run, with no separate line for peaks, tree wraps, bush nets, column wraps, a timer, or a steep pitch. Times each extra separately from the entered counts, so a house with five tree wraps and three peaks prices differently from one with none.
Gives the crew a rate to quote, not a number to check a quote against when an owner asks to match a cheaper hang-only special on a full-service job. Reports the walk-away price and the extra-work share of the job, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before the crew commits to it.

Three eaves, the same per-foot special

Using this calculator's own shipped presets, at its own shipped shop rates ($32/hr crew wage, 30% payroll burden, 15% overhead on direct cost, a 20% target margin, $55 travel and equipment):

JobThis calculator's priceThe flat $3/LF specialGap
140 LF, 1-story C9 hang-only, customer-owned lights — the job the $3/LF special is built on$539.43 bid price; $431.54 break-even cost$420.00The special prices $11.54 below this job's own break-even cost — before a dollar of profit.
160 LF, 1-story hang-and-takedown with 4 bushes and a timer$1,236.73 bid price; $989.38 break-even cost$480.00The special prices $509.38 below break-even and $756.73 below the calculator's own bid.
200 LF, 2-story full-service Victorian: icicle lights, 5 peaks, 3 trees, 8 bushes, 4 columns, timer, steep pitch, storage$4,822.33 bid price; $3,857.86 break-even cost$600.00The special prices $3,257.86 below break-even and $4,222.33 below the calculator's own bid.

The flat special is a fixed $3.00/LF, not derived from any of the three jobs. It does not clear even the cheapest one: a 1-story hang-only ranch on customer-owned C9, hung once with no January trip, is the job a $3/LF postcard rate is set on, and it still prices below this calculator's own break-even cost at these shop rates. Run your own house's numbers in the calculator to see where it falls.

A flat special is not wrong because it is simple — it is wrong when it is applied without checking it against a real cost base, and nothing about a per-foot postcard rate tells you when that has happened. This calculator does not replace judgment about your market; it replaces the arithmetic a flat rate skips.

Common questions

Why does a flat $3/LF Christmas light special get a bid wrong?

Because the cost driver is scope, stories, and extras, not "lineal feet of eave" alone. A 1-story hang-only on customer-owned C9 with no January trip is a different job from a 2-story full-service icicle install with take-down and off-season storage, and a flat per-foot number cannot see which one it is looking at.

What does a flat per-foot special usually leave out entirely?

The January take-down trip, off-season storage, the second ladder set a two-story eave needs, and every peak, tree wrap, bush net, and column wrap. A published hang rate is set on the cheapest run — a ground-reachable ranch, hang-only, customer-owned lights — and has nowhere to put the hours for a second visit, a taller ladder or a lift, or the extras a postcard special never itemizes.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

On this calculator's own shipped presets, at its own shipped shop rates ($32/hr crew wage, 30% burden, 15% overhead, a 20% target margin, $55 travel and equipment): a 140-foot 1-story hang-only ranch — the job a $3/LF special is built on — has a $431.54 break-even cost against a $420.00 flat price, already below break-even before a dollar of profit. A 160-foot hang-and-takedown job with some bushes prices at $1,236.73 against a $480.00 flat price, a $756.73 gap. A 200-foot 2-story full-service Victorian with icicle lights, peaks, trees, and storage prices at $4,822.33 against a $600.00 flat price, a $4,222.33 gap.

Is a flat per-foot rate ever the right way to quote holiday lights?

Not on this calculator's own numbers, even for the cheapest job the rate is built on: a 1-story hang-only ranch already prices below its own break-even cost at a flat $3/LF, before take-down, storage, a second story, or a single extra enters the bid. The rate is not close on a hard case — it is short on the easy one.

Does this calculator know what to charge in my market?

No. It has no data on local rates or what competitors charge. It takes the eave footage, scope, stories, light type, extras, and your loaded labor and overhead, and turns them into a walk-away price and extra-work share for the job you describe — the arithmetic a flat rate skips, not a market survey.

← Holiday Light Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. RealGreen

Two different shapes: RealGreen is business-management software for running a holiday lighting company's marketing, inventory, scheduling, and job history across a season. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this one house cost, given its eave footage, trees, access, and takedown, before you quote it.

What each tool is for

RealGreen sells business management software with a product line aimed specifically at holiday light installation companies. Its published description of that line covers marketing services, inventory management, estimating and scheduling, and job tracking — the operational spine of a company that installs lights for a few hundred properties between October and January. It is sold as an ongoing account for a business, not a single-job tool. RealGreen's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's plan names or dollar figures, so none is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — business-management software for the holiday lighting trade — are stated, and no dollar amount for RealGreen appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what RealGreen does. It does not market your services, hold your inventory, route your crews, or keep a customer record on a server. It takes one property's eave linear feet, tree, bush and column counts, storeys and roof pitch, an access premium for the runs that need a ladder set three times, material cost per linear foot, the takedown-to-hang labour ratio, off-season storage, loaded wage and payroll burden, overhead, travel, and target margin, and turns that into the per-job price and the walk-away price below which the job loses money — plus, if you already have a number on the table, a check of whether it clears that floor, and a printable customer proposal for that one job. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

Most holiday lighting contractors get different value from each: RealGreen (or a comparable platform) for running marketing, inventory, scheduling and job history across a company and a season, and a private calculator like this one for an instant, no-login gut-check on what one house should cost before a business system is involved. This page's own figures are a pricing model, not a scheduled job, an invoice, or a signed proposal.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off — which matters on a driveway in December.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or RealGreen?

They do different jobs, and a holiday lighting business of any size may end up using both. RealGreen sells business management software with a product line aimed at holiday light installation companies: marketing services, inventory management, estimating and scheduling, and job tracking, run as an ongoing account for the whole company. This calculator does one narrower thing: starting from eave linear feet, tree and bush and column counts, the number of stories and whether the roof is steep, an access premium for hard runs, material cost per linear foot, the takedown-to-hang labour ratio, off-season storage, loaded wage and payroll burden, overhead, travel, and target margin, it turns that into the per-job price and the walk-away price below which the job loses money. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type. A lighting company already running marketing, inventory, scheduling and job history across a full crew and a full season is better served by RealGreen or a comparable platform; an installer who wants an instant, private gut-check on what one house should cost before opening a business system is in the right place here.

Does this calculator handle takedown and storage?

Yes, and they are usually where a holiday lighting bid goes wrong. Takedown is entered as a ratio of the hang labour rather than a flat guess, because a crew that took eight hours to hang a roofline does not take eight hours to pull it down. Storage is entered as its own line so that the months the product sits in your building between seasons are priced rather than absorbed. Both feed the same walk-away price as the hang labour, so a bid that looks profitable on hang day and loses money in January shows up before you send it.
